Should Refiners Postpone Maintenance During a Diesel Crisis?

When diesel is scarce and margins are strong, every planned maintenance day appears to sacrifice valuable output.

...

One large turnaround can change a regional vessel programme.

Product-tanker effects move in the opposite direction

When a refinery stops, its diesel, gasoline, jet, or naphtha exports decline.

...

Moving a turnaround can lose the original resources and create a longer future outage.
War-related aviation, customs, and supply-chain disruption can make rescheduling harder. The value of an available team belongs in the decision.

Product yield complicates the run incentive

A refinery cannot produce only diesel. Higher crude runs also make gasoline, fuel oil, LPG, naphtha, and other products, whose margins may be weaker. Tight jet demand can encourage kerosene yield at the expense of gasoil.
The optimal run reflects the whole barrel and unit constraints, not the diesel price alone.

Saudi Arabia Expands Oil Storage in Japan to 24 Million Barrels

FxBrokerTrust

Summary
Japan's METI and Saudi Arabia announced on 20 November that Japan will buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its strategic reserves, while offering Saudi Arabia an additional 16 million barrels of storage, tripling its capacity in Japan to about 24 million barrels. Saudi Arabia accounted for 42% of Japan's crude imports in 2025.
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry ( METI ) and Saudi Arabia issued a joint statement on 20 November announcing an expansion of oil storage cooperation: Japan will purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its national petroleum reserves, while providing Saudi Arabia with an additional 16 million barrels of storage capacity. Combined with the kingdom's existing 8 million barrels of storage, its capacity in Japan will triple to around 24 million barrels.
Japan is topping up its emergency reserves with Saudi crude and granting Riyadh three times as much storage space within its borders, signalling that this year's Gulf supply disruptions are pushing buyers and sellers towards deeper supply cooperation.

Key Points of the Agreement

* Japan will purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its strategic petroleum reserves, subject to favourable market conditions and the completion of necessary domestic procedures;
* Saudi Arabia will gain an additional 16 million barrels of storage space in Japan on top of its existing 8 million barrels, bringing the total to around 24 million barrels;
* In 2025, Saudi Arabia accounted for 42% of Japan's crude imports, closely followed by the United Arab Emirates at 41%;
* The Middle East accounts for 93% of Japan's total oil imports;
* The agreement secures supply for Japan while providing a reliable outlet for Saudi exports.

Japan's Heavy Reliance on Gulf Supply

The agreement reflects Japan's heavy dependence on Gulf supply. In 2025, Saudi Arabia was Japan's largest source of crude imports, accounting for 42% of the total. Overall, oil from the Middle East made up 93% of Japan's imports, making the country one of the major consumers most exposed to supply disruptions in the region.
That vulnerability was tested this year, when conflict in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and forced consuming nations to draw on emergency reserves. Replenishing those stockpiles has now become a priority for importers, and long-term supply relationships offer a route to rebuilding reserves with greater certainty.
This is a mutually beneficial arrangement. For Japan, a larger and more durable link with its biggest supplier helps secure access to crude in times of crisis. For Saudi Arabia, storing oil in Japan provides a reliable destination for its exports and positions crude close to a major Asian buyer, enabling faster delivery when supply chains elsewhere come under strain.

Storage Cooperation Model May Spread

Japan's purchase of up to 8 million barrels is modest relative to global crude trade flows, but it adds a measure of certain demand at a time when the market is selling off crude amid oversupply concerns. Restocking by consuming nations that drew down emergency reserves this year could lend support to near-term crude demand.
Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group ( MUFG ) expects this model to be replicated more widely. The bank believes there is room to expand existing storage facilities, and that Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern exporters are likely to gain storage access in more countries, as both producers and consumers seek to guard against a repeat of this year's supply disruptions. Should other importers strike similar arrangements, the trend would cement Middle Eastern exporters' long-term hold over Asian demand. Such deals could also help Gulf exporters lock in demand as shipments recover, against a backdrop of oil prices pressured by expectations of oversupply.

Japan has agreed to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude for its national petroleum reserve if market conditions are favorable, the two countries said Friday.

The buyer is Lockheed Martin, the PAC-3 MSE prime, and the order covers the dual-pulse motors and ignition safety devices essential to Lockheed's production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors.
Northrop describes the work as a multi-year award and folds it into what it calls its "broader $3 billion landmark agreements announced in August". A company spokesperson told Defense Daily that Lockheed awarded the contract in mid-to-late October, weeks before the public announcement.

What the $1.6 Billion PAC-3 MSE Order Buys

The order pays for two things: the dual-pulse solid rocket motor that propels the PAC-3 MSE, and the ignition safety devices that go with it. Northrop's Allegany Ballistics Laboratory (ABL) in Rocket Center manufactures the motor, which the company says provides "maneuverability and extended range to counter evolving threats."
The spokesperson told Defense Daily that early production under the contract has already started and that the work is expected to last at least through the current seven-year framework agreement between Lockheed Martin and the Pentagon. Northrop declined to disclose how many motors it plans to build during the ramp. The spokesperson called the planned ramp "significant" and said it will support the Army's anticipated growth in annual PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 units to thousands "in the near term."
Lockheed had already signaled the order. On its Oct. 25 quarterly earnings call, CEO Jim Taiclet said that since the quarter closed the company had awarded a "$1.6 billion contract to Northrop Grumman for propulsion and other missile components", according to Defense Daily.

How the Northrop Award Fits the PAC-3 Production Surge

Defense Daily describes the Northrop order as a downstream effect of the Defense Department's framework agreements to expand production of the interceptor, and it lays out the sequence:
* In January, Lockheed Martin and the Defense Department signed a seven-year framework agreement aimed at raising annual PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 to 2,000 interceptors.
* In April, the Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $4.76 billion contract to speed up first-year PAC-3 MSE production.
* In July, a $53.9 billion contract modification covered multiyear procurement of PAC-3 MSEs for fiscal years 2026 through 2032.
* In August, Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin and the Pentagon agreed to a $2 billion framework agreement intended to triple PAC-3 MSE production through solid rocket motor work at ABL.
The prime contract dollars only become interceptors if the supply chain beneath Lockheed can keep up. Northrop says this order is part of its broader $3 billion in agreements announced in August, which suggests the October order moves that framework work into a purchase from the prime to its propulsion supplier. Neither source spells out the contractual mechanics, so the link between the two is best read as inference. What the sources do show is that the propulsion tier of the build-out now has a $1.6 billion order behind it.

Where the Extra Motor Capacity Comes From

What It Means for Contractors

For firms below the prime level, this award offers a view of how PAC-3 MSE money is moving. Prime contract dollars at Lockheed are showing up as large, multi-year purchases from propulsion suppliers, and Northrop expects the work to last at least through the seven-year framework rather than a single production lot. Suppliers to Northrop's propulsion operations, including makers of energetics, motor cases, insulation, nozzles, igniters and test equipment, may reasonably expect demand signals that run years out, not months, though neither source names specific subcontract opportunities.
The construction work at ABL creates a separate opening.

25, and Northrop announced it in mid-November. Because this is a subcontract from a prime rather than a direct government award, earnings calls and supplier press releases are often the first public sign of where prime dollars are flowing. Contractors competing for second- and third-tier PAC-3 MSE work should watch Lockheed and Northrop disclosures as closely as Army contract notices.
Finally, the order underscores how much the program leans on ABL. Northrop says ABL manufactures the dual-pulse motor that powers the PAC-3 MSE, and Defense Daily reports the August framework was aimed at tripling interceptor output through solid rocket motor work at that facility. That makes the pace of work at Rocket Center an important factor in how fast the whole program can grow.

Solid rocket motors: the munitions bottleneck is drawing new builders

By Fluxa First
Table of solid rocket motor capacity moves in October 2026, including Ursa Major's $137 million Navy awards, X-Bow's Navy booster agreement, L3Harris's $250 million GMLRS follow-on and new Camden plant, and the Lockheed Martin and Avio agreement.

Key takeaways

* In October 2026 alone, L3Harris opened a Camden, Arkansas motor plant designed to double capacity and won a $250 million GMLRS follow-on that the company says is its highest quantity in program history.
* Lockheed Martin signed with Avio, whose US unit is building a Virginia plant as part of more than $500 million of US capacity investment.
* Newer companies also won Navy work, with Ursa Major receiving $137 million and X-Bow an agreement worth up to $69.7 million that includes tooling for a 500-motor-a-year line.
* More suppliers, merchant capacity and modern manufacturing make the propulsion base more resilient, and the bottleneck is now qualification and scale, not ideas.
Precision munitions and interceptors depend on a component most people never think about: the solid rocket motor. Demand has surged, and supply has struggled to keep up; X-Bow’s chief executive described it this month as a production bottleneck decades in the making. October 2026 showed how quickly that is changing. In a single month, an incumbent opened a new plant and won a record order, a European specialist signed with Lockheed Martin to build motors in Virginia, and two newer American companies won Navy contracts. For anyone watching the American industrial base, propulsion is where capacity is being rebuilt fastest.

What happened in October?

Table of October 2026 solid rocket motor moves: Ursa Major $137M Navy awards on Oct. 5, X-Bow Navy booster agreement worth up to $69.7M on Oct. 8, L3Harris $250M GMLRS follow-on on Oct. 12, Lockheed Martin and Avio agreement on Oct. 13, and L3Harris opening its Camden, Arkansas plant on Oct. 20.
* Ursa Major, October 5. The Navy awarded Ursa Major $137 million across two contracts: $91 million for a 7-inch motor for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile and $46 million for a 10-inch motor for the Naval Modular Missile. The company says both use its Lynx approach, combining expanded energetics capacity with additive manufacturing, and that the CAAM motor is being developed with the same methods planned for full production, while the NMM motor is designed for high-rate production.
* X-Bow Systems, October 8. X-Bow won a prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop and qualify a booster for a Navy next-generation weapon program, with $50 million obligated at award. It includes production-rate tooling at its Luling, Texas site, where it plans a line for up to 500 motors a year. X-Bow said it recently finished its first major production contract, delivering more than 2,100 motors.
* L3Harris, October 12. L3Harris received a $250 million follow-on from Lockheed Martin for standard-range GMLRS propulsion, the highest quantity in the program’s history, according to the company.
* Lockheed Martin and Avio, October 13. The two companies announced a cooperation agreement under which, after qualification, Avio USA’s new plant in Hurt, Virginia will produce motors for Extended Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile. Avio says it is investing more than $500 million in US capacity to become a merchant supplier to several defense customers.
* L3Harris, October 20. L3Harris opened its Arsenal of Freedom plant in Camden, Arkansas, designed to double current GMLRS motor capacity with room to grow. It was built under a $216 million Defense Production Act Title III agreement signed in 2023, and the company says it is building about 60 new facilities across four states.

Why does this matter for sovereignty?

A country that cannot produce enough propulsion cannot sustain its own defense or support its allies. The same industrial skills, energetic materials, casting propellant, case manufacturing and testing, also matter for space launch and hypersonics. When only a few suppliers make a critical component, demand spikes are hard to absorb.

...

What should founders and investors take from this?

Energetics is hard. Facilities need safety distances, permits and specialized equipment. Qualification takes years of testing. That is exactly why the companies that get through it build real moats. Lessons that apply well beyond propulsion:
1. Production is the product. Customers buy rate and reliability, not a single impressive test.
2. Qualification is a milestone to plan and fund , not an afterthought.
3. Early government contracts can finance capacity , but founders should plan for the commercial or multi-customer business that follows.
4. Adjacent markets matter. Space launch and hypersonics draw on the same skills and can diversify revenue.
We covered parallel shifts in the drone components industrial base , castings and forgings and qualified manufacturing capacity .

How we see it

Defense is one of several areas where we build and invest, and propulsion is a clear example of the broader pattern we care about: essential, hard-to-make components where American capacity fell behind demand. The answer is not one more prime contract. It is a deeper base of durable companies, incumbents and new entrants alike, that can design for production, qualify quickly and keep shipping. October suggests that base is finally being built.

Frequently asked questions

Why are solid rocket motors a bottleneck?

Solid rocket motors power many US tactical missiles and interceptors, as well as some space launch boosters. Making them requires energetic materials, specialized facilities, strict safety processes and long qualification. When demand surges, capacity limits show up quickly, which is why the Pentagon is funding new plants and new entrants.

What is a merchant supplier of solid rocket motors?

A merchant supplier sells motors to several prime contractors rather than building only for its own missiles. Avio says its US investment is aimed at becoming a merchant supplier to various defense customers, which gives primes more options and adds competition.

UK Tests Found No RDX in Explosives Bought for Ukraine

Miles Johnson · Financial Times · Tuesday, November 24, 2026 · 4 min read
The Financial Times’ Miles Johnson reports that Britain’s Ministry of Defence paid tens of millions of pounds to US supplier Tripwire for explosives intended for Ukraine, but testing found no RDX, a key ingredient of conventional C-4. Johnson says the product appears instead to have been a cheaper commercial explosive sold under a new name, at a markup of as much as 100 per cent. Tripwire and its salesman deny the findings, while the MoD says the explosives performed as expected.

The dispute is over what Britain contracted to buy

Britain’s Ministry of Defence bought explosives from Tripwire, an American supplier, for shipment to Ukraine. The central dispute is whether the products contained RDX, a key ingredient of conventional C-4, as Tripwire claimed—or whether the company sold a different, cheaper commercial explosive under a new name.
Miles Johnson of the Financial Times says the MoD signed contracts with Tripwire worth tens of millions of pounds over almost three years. The explosives travelled from a factory in Kentucky to Ukraine, where they were to be packed into attack drones. A Ministry of Defence letter shown in the investigation identifies Enhanced Demolition Compound-4, or EDC-4, in 1.25-pound blocks and says the intended user was Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence. It names Tripwire International as exporter and says authorised UK representatives would collect the explosives after approval of US export regulations.
Tripwire marketed EDC-4 as a more powerful version of the traditional M112 demolition block. Its product description said the compound combined conventional RDX and nitrocellulose with a proprietary blend of PETN and atomized aluminum. Tripwire claimed those additions increased detonation velocity, breaking force and blast pressure. The company’s website described it as an internationally recognized leader in explosive products, services and training.
The investigation identifies Ryan Morris as an American explosives salesman and a previously bankrupt part-time policeman from rural Pennsylvania, and links him to Tripwire. The FT showed promotional material featuring Morris in a suit holding an explosive device against a backdrop of armed soldiers and military vehicles. Johnson says the FT traced the supply chain from a factory in the southern United States to Ukraine.

Tripwire’s specification and the test results diverge

The FT’s supply-chain analysis and chemical testing pointed to a different product, Johnson says: an existing white-label commercial explosive that Morris appears to have rebranded and sold to Britain at a markup of as much as 100 percent. The investigation found that the product contained a cheaper explosive instead of RDX.
The comparison shown in the investigation sets out what Tripwire listed for EDC-4 alongside conventional C-4. Its EDC-4 column includes PETN, aluminum powder, nitrocellulose, proprietary amounts of RDX and plasticizer, and a taggant. The conventional C-4 column lists 89–92 percent RDX, 8–11 percent plasticizer and a taggant. The displayed figures give EDC-4 a detonation velocity of 28,000 feet per second, against 26,400 for traditional C-4.
* Product | Composition shown in Tripwire’s comparison | Detonation velocity shown
* Traditional C-4 | RDX (89–92%), plasticizer (8–11%), taggant (>1%) | 26,400 ft/s
* Tripwire EDC-4 | PETN, aluminum powder, nitrocellulose, proprietary RDX and plasticizer, taggant (>1%) | 28,000 ft/s
Tripwire’s comparison lists proprietary RDX in EDC-4; the FT’s reported testing found none.
That specification differs from the reported test results. Johnson says the FT’s chemical testing found no RDX and identified a different, cheaper explosive with different safety characteristics. The MoD also performed multiple independent tests that found no RDX. The FT’s reporting says this conflicts with Tripwire’s displayed composition and safety data sheet, which names RDX and PETN while withholding exact percentages as a trade secret.
The safety sheet describes EDC-4 as a malleable plastic explosive demolition block. It classifies it as an explosive with a mass-explosion hazard and warns that it is toxic if swallowed. The discrepancy matters because the explosives were shipped into an active war zone, where the supplier’s safety information was relevant to their use.
Tripwire and Morris strongly deny the FT’s findings. They insist that, to their knowledge, every batch supplied to the MoD contained RDX.

The MoD’s performance defence leaves the premium unexplained

The MoD has defended the purchases, saying the explosives performed as expected. Johnson says the department has not explained why it paid a substantial premium to an American middleman for what the FT describes as a simple product, or why the supplier’s safety documents appear to be contradicted by its own test results.
But it hasn't been able to explain why it paid the American middleman seen in these eye-catching videos such a substantial premium for a simple product, or why the supplier safety documents for high explosives shipped into an active war zone appear to be contradicted by the MoD's own testing.

Pentagon's 60,000 Attack Drones Hit a 1940s Explosives Bottleneck

Haye Kesteloo · Editor-in-Chief October 28, 2026 · 21:32 ET 4 min read
US Army sergeant in camouflage body armor lowering white Fat Shark FPV goggles over his eyes in a field of heather
A US Army team leader with NATO's Forward Land Forces Battle Group Poland prepares his FPV goggles before a drone launch at Bemowo Piskie Training Area, August 2026. Photo credit: US Army Reserve, Staff Sgt. Emilie Lenglain
The Pentagon has committed to buying 60,000 attack drones, and the Wall Street Journal reports that the United States does not make enough explosives to arm them. All U.S. production of HMX and RDX, two powerful military explosives, comes from a single plant in Tennessee that was built during World War II.
A new joint venture called Odin Energetics wants to change that. Chemicals maker Solugen and warhead builder Kraken Kinetics announced it this month and committed $115 million. Odin says it can start supplying the military in small quantities next year.
The Army’s own fix is running late. Its $1 billion modernization of that Tennessee plant was due in 2025 and now targets 2029 or later.

Drone Dominance Needs a Warhead for Nearly Every Drone It Buys

Drone Dominance is the Pentagon’s $1.1 billion program to field low-cost drones by the end of 2027. A department official told the Wall Street Journal that virtually all of its 60,000 committed attack drones are designed to carry explosives. The payload order is nearly as large as the airframe order.

...

Holston Army Ammunition Plant in Kingsport, Tennessee, has been the only U.S. producer of HMX and RDX since widespread closures of government-owned plants in the 1990s. Tyler Hacker of the Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments estimates the 84-year-old plant now runs at about 3% of its 1944 peak.
Industry experts told the Journal the wait for Holston product runs one to two years, and the paper reports the plant has been beset by explosions and pollution violations. BAE Systems, which operates it, referred questions about the plant to the Army, which owns it. Army spokeswoman Ellen Lovett said the upgrade timeline shifted to ensure safety and technical standards were being met, and that the service is proceeding with safety and other improvements.
For now there are few other options. European explosives are going to Ukraine or staying home for rearmament, and many of the ingredients the U.S. once bought from Russia and China are now under export restrictions. The Army announced a $903 million research facility in Kentucky in March to raise HMX and RDX output before 2031, and the Pentagon set up a new office for energetics production.
It is the production gap Anduril’s Brian Schimpf spent nine years warning about , seen from the explosives end. Kraken Kinetics CEO Brian Davis, an Odin co-founder, put the timeline bluntly: “We have actually been in an energetics crisis for 20 years.”

Odin Says It Can Make About a Tenth of Holston’s Output

Odin says it can already produce close to a tenth of the roughly 11 million pounds of HMX and RDX that Holston makes each year, in modular factories that the Wall Street Journal reports can be built in about six months and set up at bases, test sites or battlefields.
Odin’s website calls its shipping-container factory Nitroforge . Solugen, whose largest investor is Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, ships the starting chemicals by ordinary truck, and the explosive is only produced at Odin’s site. Executives pitch that as a safety answer to an industry where accidents have killed workers and shut plants for months, and as a way around local opposition to bomb factories.
At a test range just over an hour from Houston, Odin detonated a new formulation its makers say is 30% more powerful than what the military currently puts on drones. That figure is the company’s own.
The Army, which is looking at bringing energetics production onto its bases, is in discussions with Odin about supplying advanced explosives. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, a lending office, has discussed possible funding with the company, executives said.

Warheads are where the drone boom meets energetics. The winners of the Pentagon's spring 2026 Drone Dominance Lethality Prize Challenge, Bravo Ordnance, Kela, Kraken Kinetics, Mountain Horse Solutions and Northrop Grumman, became preferred payload providers for Gauntlet drone makers, and most of them are startups. By Hannah Miller (Defence Industry Europe)

Pentagon says Defense Logistics Agency directed $2 billion to stockpile critical materials
Photo: U.S. Marine Corps.
The U.S. Defense Logistics Agency committed $2 billion in fiscal 2026 to buy strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile. Most of its critical mineral contracts were aimed at supporting domestic production by giving U.S. suppliers a clearer idea of what the government will buy, said Eric Mata, director of DLA Strategic Materials.
The stockpile is meant to cover shortfalls when commercial suppliers cannot meet military and essential civilian needs during a national emergency. The materials range from high-purity aluminum to vanadium pentoxide and are used in aerospace, shipbuilding, communications, space systems and munitions.
Mata said buying from U.S. suppliers matters most when a material is hard to replace and few reliable sources can supply it in the quantities or forms needed. “In those cases, domestic acquisition and stockpiling can help reduce single-point-of-failure risks, sustain U.S. industrial capability and preserve material availability during disruption,” he said.
The agency’s purchases support a National Defense Strategy priority of bringing strategic industries back to the United States and expanding domestic production. Mata said the stockpile complements other federal investments while reducing reliance on foreign producers, long shipping routes and suppliers concentrated in a few locations.
Mining is one source of critical materials, but recovery and recycling can also supply them. Mata said recovering materials domestically can give manufacturers another source of supply where the process is technically and economically viable.
“These efforts are helping domestic companies plan production, retain skilled workers and expand capacity where economically viable,” Mata said. More predictable orders can also help suppliers keep specialized production capabilities in place, he said.

Middle East conflict revives Pentagon concerns over US high-purity aluminium supply
Stock image for referential purposes only
A Pentagon-led simulation has brought fresh attention to the US’ dependence on imported high-purity aluminium, a critical raw material used in military aircraft, armoured vehicles and other defence applications. Conducted months before recent disruptions spurred by the Middle East conflict, the exercise had the US aluminium supply chain in focus.
It examined how the US aluminium supply chain would respond during a major geopolitical conflict and identified high-purity aluminium as one of the most exposed segments of the country’s defence industrial base. The findings have gained renewed relevance following the Iranian missile attacks on the aluminium facilities of Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA) and Aluminium Bahrain (Alba) in the Middle East or Gulf region on March 28, 2026.
Although repairs are running a head of schedule and production has since resumed at some plants, supply routes and output recovery remain under close watch , highlighting the importance of resilient aluminium supply chains for strategic industries.

Heavy reliance on imported high-purity aluminium
According to the exercise report, the simulation concluded that the US remains heavily reliant on overseas suppliers for high-purity aluminium. While China dominates global primary aluminium production, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has emerged as the principal supplier of the ultra-refined grade imported into the US, accounting for an estimated 90 per cent of imports used for defence-related applications.
High-purity aluminium contains exceptionally low levels of iron and silicon, making it suitable for manufacturing specialised alloys used in fighter aircraft and other defence equipment.
The exercise also highlighted a structural challenge for the US market. Domestic large-scale production of high-purity aluminium effectively ended in 2022 after the country’s last major producer ceased operations due to rising energy costs. As defence demand increases globally, restoring domestic capacity by stockpiling high-purity aluminium and associated products has become a growing topic of discussion among policymakers and industry participants.
Bill Greenwalt, Senior Fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Industrial Policy, described the situation as “a huge wake-up call for the department to be looking at supply chains in all areas around the world to ensure that they’re not especially vulnerable to attack or sabotage.”
Industry sources say that the market is not facing an outright shortage, but primary aluminium supplies remain tight . Much of the material used by US defence manufacturers seems to be sourced from EGA, before being processed by companies such as Kaiser Aluminum, Constellium and Arconic.
Commenting on the market, Uday Patel, Senior Research Manager for global aluminium markets at Wood Mackenzie, said, “We’re in a situation where there is no solution. Much will depend on how much stocks are in the pipeline.”

Policy recommendations focus on rebuilding domestic capacity
The war game, held over two days in July 2025 and overseen by the Institute for Defense Analyses, asked participants to assess how the US aluminium industry could respond if imports were disrupted during a large-scale conflict while domestic production also faced unexpected outages.
Participants recommended building strategic reserves of high-purity aluminium, expanding domestic production, investing in additional processing capacity and improving access to reliable, affordable power, an essential requirement for aluminium production.
The exercise forms part of wider efforts by the US government to identify vulnerabilities in critical mineral and manufacturing supply chains. Alongside supply diversification, policymakers are also examining ways to strengthen visibility across lower-tier suppliers that support the defence sector.
Charles Johnson, President and CEO of the Aluminum Association, said the findings reinforce the close relationship between industrial capability and national security, stating that “America’s military readiness is inseparable from America’s industrial readiness.” The association continues to advocate measures aimed at strengthening domestic aluminium production and processing.
Recent US policy initiatives like higher aluminium tariffs and incentives for new smelting capacity echo those objectives. However, industry observers note that establishing new high-purity aluminium production will require substantial investment, long development timelines and access to competitive energy supplies.
As geopolitical risks continue to influence global metals markets, the Pentagon exercise has highlighted the strategic importance of securing reliable sources of high-purity aluminium while gradually rebuilding domestic manufacturing capability to support long-term defence requirements.

Pentagon’s stockpile and Project Vault risk bidding war for scarce critical minerals

* November 12, 2026
* By The Oregon Group
* the Pentagon’s Defense Logistics Agency committed US$2 billion in the 2026 fiscal year to buy critical minerals for the National Defense Stockpile, including tungsten and cobalt, and has requested US$18 billion for the 2027 fiscal year
* Project Vault, a US$12 billion commercial reserve built on a US$10 billion loan from the Export-Import Bank of the United States, can hold all 60 minerals on the US critical minerals list, so it overlaps with every metal the Pentagon is buying
* the two reserves are meant to do different jobs, one for war and one for the market shocks before a war, but they compete for the same kinds of material in thin markets for rare earths, antimony, germanium, cobalt and tungsten, where China refines more than 90% of the world’s rare earths and gallium
* they are not the only buyers: the Pentagon has put US$750 million behind buying rare earth carbonate from Brazil’s Serra Verde for dysprosium, terbium, neodymium and praseodymium, while the US International Development Finance Corporation has approved US$1.5 billion for a minerals fund that can also buy output

...

In March 2025 it sought bids for cobalt, copper, nickel and lithium for its reserves, as we showed when the US launched its US$12 billion strategic minerals stockpile :
Bar chart of cobalt purchased by China's state stockpiling agency in 2015, 2016, 2020, 2022 and 2023, with 2023 the record year, plus Darton Commodities' low and high forecasts for 2024. Source: Darton Commodities, Bloomberg.
For example, the world mined about 85,000 tonnes of tungsten last year, 67,000 tonnes of it in China. Amid new export controls and strong demand, tungsten prices rose x6 between January 2025 and April 2026.
In most of the minerals both reserves want, one country supplies the bulk of world mine output, US Geological Survey data show:
China dominates share of top refining country for 20 energy related minerals - The Oregon Group
And demand is rising fast. Demand for copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths has grown by close to 10% a year on average, against about 1% for aluminium, lead and zinc, according to the International Energy Agency. Electric vehicles, battery storage, grids and magnets drive that growth, while defence, aerospace and the servers inside artificial intelligence data centres add more.
“Given the highly concentrated nature of supply and the relatively small size of these markets, small shifts in supply patterns or purchasing behaviour had an outsized impact on prices,” the International Energy Agency said.
Meanwhile, buyers outside China already pay several times more than Chinese buyers for some of these metals, the agency found :
Bar chart comparing European prices with Chinese domestic prices: gallium about x5, heavy rare earths about x5, germanium about x3. Source: International Energy Agency.

...

There is little sign yet that they work together, so the money could build new mines and refineries, or simply bid up the price of what already exists, and the companies the reserves are meant to protect are already warning about the second.

Two stockpiles, two jobs

The National Defense Stockpile (NDS) is the Pentagon’s emergency store. US law says its purpose “is to serve the interest of national defense only” and that it “is not to be used for economic or budgetary purposes”, the Congressional Research Service notes. The stockpile’s own notices go further: “It is not intended to influence prices in the market or insulate private industry from supply shocks.”
It held assets of US$1.3 billion in March 2023, against a 1989 peak of US$9.6 billion across 91 items, according to the National Academies .

...

There also appears to be no official statement of how the two buyers coordinate, so the two programmes are “not interdependent” , according to Fastmarkets.

The other US buyers in the queue

The defence stockpile and Project Vault are the only two US programmes built to hold critical minerals in reserve, but they are not the only government-backed buyers in these markets.
Pentagon offtakes: under its July 2025 deal with MP Materials, the Pentagon agreed that for 10 years “100% of the magnets produced at the 10X Facility will be purchased by defense and commercial customers”, alongside a US$110 per kilogram floor price for neodymium-praseodymium “stockpiled or sold”, the company said .

...

In June 2026, G7 leaders agreed to “cooperate on stockpiling and crisis management and establish a joint cooperation mechanism”, according to the summit annex . These deals could ease competition between allies, but they also add more state buyers to the same markets.

What could prove this wrong

The clash is not inevitable.
For example, Elmet does not intend to deliver tungsten into the stockpile until new supply from the mines and processing it is backing becomes available, so the stockpile adds to supply rather than taking from factories. The Pentagon’s 10-year floor price for MP Materials’ neodymium-praseodymium works the same way, by giving a new producer a reason to build.
That only holds if Vault pays for new, non-Chinese output. It has published no such rule, and Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy warns that fast emergency access “would require sourcing many critical minerals from China”. “In essence then, the stockpile would source from China to absorb a shock from China,” the center said .
And new supply is slow to arrive, as we wrote in our earlier article on the Pentagon’s China minerals ban :
“A new mine or refining source to replace that supply can take up to 10 years to identify, build and certify”

Conclusion

The US now has a reserve for war and a reserve for the war before the war. If the two are run as one system, they can pull new mines and refineries into being; if they are not, they will bid against each other, and against Japan and Europe, for the same scarce tonnes, and drive up prices for the manufacturers Vault was set up to protect.

The US Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) has committed $2 billion to acquire strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile throughout the fiscal year.
The National Defense Stockpile helps reduce the risk that material shortages could affect national defense and essential civilian industries. Strategic and critical materials needed to meet military, industrial and essential civilian requirements during a national emergency, but aren’t available commercially in sufficient quantities include rare earths, tungsten, titanium and antimony.
Most of the critical mineral contracts awarded through DLA’s Contracting Services Office were targeted demand signals to enable domestic production and to support the National Defense Strategy emphasis on resilient, secure supply chains, Director of DLA Strategic Materials Eric Mata said.
“Domestic sourcing is especially important when a material is essential to national defense, is subject to concentrated or vulnerable supply chains, is difficult to replace, and is not readily available from reliable sources in the quantities or forms required,” Mata said in a news release. “In those cases, domestic acquisition and stockpiling can help reduce single-point-of-failure risks, sustain U.S. industrial capability, and preserve material availability during disruption.”
Materials sourced for the stockpile can range from high-purity aluminum to vanadium pentoxide, with many elements, metals and compounds in between. Outside of mining, approaches like recovery, recycling, refining and processing can also produce these materials. Where it’s technically and economically feasible, domestic reclamation strengthens supply resilience by providing secondary sources of critical materials, Mata said.
The National Defense Strategy calls for supporting the defense industrial base through reshoring strategic industries and expanding domestic production.
DLA’s acquisitions for the National Defense Stockpile direct demand toward American material suppliers and processors, strengthening industrial readiness and resilience, Mata said.
“These materials support a range of industrial capabilities across aerospace, maritime, ground, space, communications and munitions-related sectors,” he said.
Stockpiled materials reduce defense industrial base uncertainty and provide demand signals that help sustain specialized capabilities, Mata said. They work alongside other War Department and federal projects to strengthen domestic critical-material supply chains to complement — rather than replace — other investment options.
He also noted the national security benefits of stockpiling to reduce exposure to foreign supply risk by lowering reliance on overseas producers, long transportation routes, and geographically concentrated supply chains.
“These efforts are helping domestic companies plan production, retain skilled workers and expand capacity where economically viable,” Mata said. “By pairing targeted acquisitions with domestic sourcing and broader industrial-base investments, DLA Strategic Materials is helping build a more resilient supply chain for materials important to national defense.”

Summary Description 1
Islanded, cybersecure microgrids and decentralized power generation across five Japanese military installations are being planned by USACE Japan District with the USMC. The portfolio targets 14+ days of mission operations without commercial grid power, with an anticipated $380 million–$600 million acquisition magnitude. The Government anticipates an OTA using a Construction Manager at Risk delivery model, with CMMC Level 1 anticipated.

Scope

The contractor would support preconstruction and, if authorized, final design and construction for five microgrid and power-generation projects. Work includes constructability reviews, value engineering, schedule optimization, open-book cost modeling, utility interconnections, controls, commissioning, and cybersecurity. The projects use solar PV, diesel or gas generation, battery storage, microgrid controllers, and related civil, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, communications, and facility work.

Deliverables

* • P-904 at CATC Camp Fuji: 400 kW solar PV, 800 kW peaker generation or BESS, 400 kW standby diesel generation, controls, cybersecurity, and commissioning.

...

* • P-406 at Camp Courtney: 4,000-square-foot generator facility, 5,000 kW diesel generation, 1,685 kW solar PV, 2,400 kW four-hour BESS, site work, communications improvements, commissioning, and RMF accreditation.
* • Phase 1 preconstruction services and a proposed Guaranteed Maximum Price after approximately 95% to 100% design. Construction execution would proceed only if the GMP is accepted.

Eligibility & set-aside

This notice is voluntary market research, not a solicitation. CMMC Level 1 is anticipated. The stated NAICS code is 236220 for market-research purposes, and the notice says OTA requirements are not subject to FAR-based small-business regulations. No set-aside is identified in the provided solicitation facts.

Place of performance

Multiple military bases in Japan, including CATC Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture, MCAS Iwakuni in Yamaguchi Prefecture, and Camps Foster, Hansen, and Courtney in Okinawa.

Evaluation criteria

No award evaluation rule is stated because this is an RFI rather than a solicitation. The Government will use responses to assess delivery methods, commercial capabilities, host-nation supply chains, and the choice between FAR contracts and OTA.

Submission requirements

Complete the attached Market Intelligence Questionnaire. Document the response and email it to H. Christine Allen and Erica J. Stiner at the listed USACE addresses. Responses are due by 17 December 2026 at 14:00 Japan Standard Time. The Government will not reimburse response-preparation costs, and responding will not affect a firm's ability to compete if a future solicitation is issued.

This briefing outlines the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' (USACE) plan to utilize Other Transactional Authority (OTA) with Construction Manager at Risk (CM@R) delivery for upcoming Marine Corps Energy Resilience Readiness Program (ERCIP) projects in Japan. OTAs operate outside the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) under 10 U.S.C. § 2808a, offering flexibility, commercial best practices, and collaborative arrangements, while remaining subject to fiscal law, cybersecurity, and environmental regulations. The CM@R process engages the construction contractor early during design to enhance constructability, cost control, and scheduling. Procurement involves a two-step solicitation: a Request for Qualifications/White Papers, followed by interactive pitch presentations with top-ranked firms. Awards occur in two phases: Phase 1 covers negotiated preconstruction services, and Phase 2 establishes a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) for construction. If a GMP agreement is not reached, the government may competitively solicit construction elsewhere. The pipeline comprises five resilient microgrid projects in Japan: 1. Camp Fuji (FY25 P904): Target award May 2028. 2. MCAS Iwakuni (FY26 P1016): Target award Feb 2029. 3. Camp Foster (FY30 P312): Target award Feb 2029. 4. Camp Hansen (FYTBD P-625): Award TBD. 5. Camp Courtney (FYTBD P406): Award TBD. Each project involves constructing resilient energy systems integrating natural gas/diesel generators, solar photovoltaic systems, battery energy storage systems (BESS), utility interconnections, controls, commissioning, and cybersecurity to ensure uninterrupted power for warfighters.

European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers

By Martin Chomsky (Defence Industry Europe)
EU | November 23, 2026
European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
EU defence ministers have endorsed eight opportunities for military cooperation in a review that urges governments to plan capabilities together before taking national procurement decisions. The 2026 Coordinated Annual Review on Defence (CARD), approved on 17 November, identifies opportunities ranging from missiles and unmanned systems to the infrastructure needed to sustain European operations.
The report finds that agreement on defence priorities has not yet translated into a consistently collaborative approach to purchasing equipment. It recommends considering cooperation at the capability planning stage and incorporating it into national programmes and budgets, with projects prepared to draw on EU funding.
Ministers endorsed opportunities to cooperate on a family of cruise missiles, long-range artillery using multiple launch rocket systems and a family of long-range air defence interceptors. They also backed opportunities involving modular, interoperable unmanned ground vehicles and layered counter-drone systems for force protection and critical infrastructure.
The other three opportunities concern space-based early warning, detection and tracking, a European secure defence cloud and a European approach to strategic air mobility. The European Defence Agency (EDA) identifies these as strategic enablers that allow Europe to decide, act and sustain operations autonomously.
“With CARD, we have identified three collaborative opportunities related to strategic enablers,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk. “From space-based early warning to strategic air mobility, and a secure, federated defence cloud architecture, these strategic enablers are essential to strengthening Europe’s deterrence and defence capabilities.”
Their scale, cost and dependence on shared architectures and networks make cooperation necessary, the report says. It argues that no single country can develop and support them alone, while access cannot be assumed in every future contingency.
CARD calls for further analysis, stronger member-state involvement and dedicated roadmaps for these capabilities. That work should build on EDA’s activities and Priority Capability Areas, in coherence with NATO.
The report makes five recommendations covering earlier cooperation, planning beyond 2030, joint work on strategic enablers, the full process of capability development and faster adoption of innovation. It stresses that buying equipment is only part of delivering forces that can deploy and operate effectively.
Personnel, training, doctrine, logistics, sustainment and interoperability increasingly determine how much defence investment becomes usable capability. Shared training capacity, common information-sharing architectures and integration of sensors with command and control offer opportunities that can be delivered faster than large programmes.
The review also identifies delays between promising technological results and operational use. It attributes those delays to experimentation, requirements and acquisition being managed too sequentially and calls for innovation to reach the field faster.
Immediate readiness requirements must be balanced with investment in medium- and long-term needs beyond 2030. The report warns that underinvestment may become visible only after several planning cycles, when correcting it would take considerable time and money.
More systematic cooperation would give manufacturers clearer and more predictable demand, supporting production at scale and reducing supply-chain dependencies. Delivering that cooperation also requires stronger intergovernmental support for joint acquisition, capability development and research.
EDA’s strengthening process is intended to provide that support and help CARD and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) deliver results. EU incentives, including the European Defence Industry Programme, would support those efforts.
At the 17 November EDA Steering Board, ministers also endorsed a joint statement on defence security of supply. They agreed to increase the agency’s budget.
EDA prepared the report in coordination with the European External Action Service and the EU Military Staff. It is the final deliverable of the fourth CARD cycle, covering 2025–2026.

Europe’s Sovereign Cloud Market Expands as EU Procurement and New Services Challenge US Dominance

* November 24, 2026
* QuestComms
Server racks in a data centre, illustrative photograph
European cloud providers are expanding their services as governments and regulated industries seek greater control over sensitive data and critical digital infrastructure. EU procurement creates opportunities for local suppliers despite the dominance of US companies.
Europe’s campaign to reduce its dependence on non-European cloud infrastructure is gaining commercial momentum, with public-sector procurement, regulatory requirements and new technology services encouraging companies to reconsider where and how their data is stored and processed.
The European Commission has established a sovereign-cloud procurement framework worth up to €180 million over six years, allowing EU institutions and agencies to acquire cloud services that meet defined requirements concerning security, legal jurisdiction and technological independence.
The framework, awarded in April, includes European providers such as STACKIT, Scaleway and a consortium led by Post Telecom involving Clever Cloud and OVHcloud.
A further consortium led by Proximus includes partners offering specialised services and technology.
The programme is intended to encourage a market capable of providing digital infrastructure under European governance and regulatory requirements.

Sovereignty becomes a commercial consideration

Cloud sovereignty has traditionally been discussed primarily in the context of national security and public administration.
However, demand is increasingly extending to financial institutions, healthcare providers, utilities and other organisations handling commercially or legally sensitive information.
For these customers, the location of a data centre represents only one aspect of the decision.
Businesses must also consider which companies control the infrastructure, whose laws may apply, whether services can be operated independently and whether technology providers retain access to essential systems.
The Commission’s Cloud Sovereignty Framework evaluates providers against 48 criteria across eight categories.
These cover strategic and operational control, legal jurisdiction, data and artificial intelligence, supply chains, technology, security and environmental sustainability.
The framework also assigns Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Levels, distinguishing different degrees of independence and operational resilience.
For corporate buyers, these criteria offer a more detailed assessment than simply asking whether data remains physically inside the EU.

European providers expand their offerings

French technology company OVHcloud announced a package of 55 cloud and artificial intelligence products on 19 November, covering computing infrastructure, business applications and access to advanced AI processing capabilities.
The company is positioning its services as an option for organisations requiring European-hosted technology.
The announcement includes AI infrastructure and workplace tools intended to compete in markets dominated by American hyperscale cloud providers.
Other European companies are pursuing similar opportunities, often combining local hosting with specialised security or compliance arrangements.
Nevertheless, the market remains highly concentrated.
Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud collectively account for more than 70 per cent of the European cloud market, according to estimates referenced in the Commission’s work on future cloud legislation.
European providers therefore face considerable disadvantages in scale, capital investment and the breadth of services available.
Expanding market share requires more than public procurement contracts. Customers must be persuaded that alternatives can support demanding enterprise applications at competitive prices.

American companies adapt to European requirements

The response from American providers complicates the competitive picture.
Amazon has developed a European Sovereign Cloud offering designed to operate within the EU under separate governance arrangements.
Microsoft and Google have also pursued services and partnerships intended to address European data residency and sovereignty concerns.
Some arrangements combine American technology with European operators or control structures.
These models may provide additional safeguards, but they do not necessarily deliver the same degree of technological independence as an infrastructure platform developed and controlled entirely within Europe.
The Commission’s procurement assessment distinguishes between these models rather than treating all sovereign-cloud offerings as equivalent.
The emergence of competing approaches creates additional choices for businesses but also makes supplier evaluation more complex.

Infrastructure investment presents a second challenge

European cloud development also depends on access to data centres, electricity, specialised processors and investment capital.
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence is increasing demand for computing infrastructure while raising concerns about energy consumption and grid capacity.
As QuestComms has previously reported , the environmental and electricity requirements of AI infrastructure are becoming important commercial considerations.
European providers must expand computing capacity without allowing operating costs to undermine their competitiveness.
Access to advanced chips, reliable power supplies and appropriate data-centre locations will influence the speed at which new services can reach the market.

Procurement standards could reshape the industry

The Commission’s framework provides a mechanism through which public-sector demand can support suppliers offering stronger guarantees of European control.
The initiative also sits alongside the EU’s wider technology policy, including new digital investment programmes and proposals for cloud and AI infrastructure development.
However, the existence of procurement opportunities does not guarantee that European providers will displace established international suppliers.
Corporate customers will continue to evaluate cost, performance, reliability and compatibility with existing systems.
The commercial opportunity lies in providing credible alternatives for organisations with demanding sovereignty requirements.
For European cloud companies, the next stage will depend on converting regulatory interest and public procurement support into substantial, sustainable demand from private-sector customers.

Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier

Ukraine’s strikes on the Kerch Bridge and Russian navy show the extent of its defence industry’s abilities. The EU 2027 finance package should seek to boost that industry towards a lasting partnership.
Expert comment
Published 23 November 2026 — 3 minute READ
Image — Vantor satellite image shows a damaged section of the Kerch Bridge. Satellite image (c) 2026 Vantor.
### Dean Wilson Chief of the General Staff's Fellow, International Security Programme
In mid-November, Ukrainian forces destroyed a road span of the Kerch Bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia. The strike used jet-powered drones and cruise missiles reportedly guided through an airborne relay network rather than Starlink.

...

The head of Ukraine’s Council of Defence Industry has said that manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of their potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders. That suggests that additional funding could quickly unlock production potential.
However, Europe’s requirements go beyond volume. Advanced air defence, particularly against ballistic missiles, depends on complex radar and sensor networks, high-end interceptors and industrial supply chains that require substantial investment and sustained development. Ukraine’s experience can inform European capability development. But it does not remove the need for Europe to build and maintain such capabilities itself.

The limits of a supplier relationship

There are other limitations on purchasing from Ukraine. Kyiv’s export framework is designed to protect its own forces. Companies may export only if they can also fulfil Ukrainian government contracts. Exports carry no intellectual property rights. And re-export requires Kyiv’s approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax.
Even the drones built at the first Ukrainian joint venture in Germany are currently allocated to Ukraine’s armed forces. These are rational choices for a country fighting for its survival. But they mean that in a crisis, European governments could not assume Ukrainian output would be available for their own requirements, at least until Kyiv’s rules adapted.
A ceasefire would raise a different problem extending beyond supply-chain security. Ukraine’s advantage is tied to the operational environment in which its firms develop and test equipment. A settlement would necessarily reduce the operational feedback, procurement incentives and pressure that drive innovation.

...

From procurement to partnership

The European Commission’s proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027, the second half of the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, including €31.7 billion for defence, provides an opportunity to shape cooperation. The allocation of these funds will have long-term consequences beyond Ukraine’s immediate military requirements.
Funding can support Ukrainian production for domestic use, establish joint ventures on European territory, or, where EU rules allow a derogation, finance procurement from established suppliers outside Europe, including the United States.
Buying Ukrainian output sustains Ukraine’s defence. And buying from outside Europe fills immediate gaps. But only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe. Ukraine’s immediate needs, particularly for air defence this winter, must remain central to European assistance. But joint ventures are where support and European industrial development can converge, and where a meaningful share of the package should be directed.
Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems.
The partnership should rest on a division of labour that draws on what Ukraine’s circumstances have produced. The war has given Ukraine’s defence industry what European nations cannot match during peacetime: urgency, a tolerance for failure, and feedback loops that are measured in days.
Reinforced by Kyiv stripping out procurement, testing and regulatory barriers, Ukraine’s industry benefits from low-cost mass production and rapid iteration under pressure. That has delivered interceptor drones and long-range strike at a pace and cost that European procurement has, to date, struggled to match.
Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems. Ukraine is already offering foreign firms the chance to test equipment in near-combat conditions alongside frontline units, through its state-backed Brave1 defence-tech cluster, and to pair with Ukrainian manufacturers for co-production. European states should take up that offer as partners rather than customers.
European states and companies, in turn, bring radar and sensor technology, high-end interceptors, sovereign space-based communications, capital, and production sites beyond the reach of Russian missiles.
